name: Kvrocks
listed_description: A distributed key value NoSQL database that uses RocksDB as storage engine and is compatible with Redis protocol.
reason: No numeric win over a named baseline anywhere reachable. The repo moved to apache/kvrocks (4.5k stars, Apache-2.0); its README has features, build and namespace text only, and states the aim to 'decrease the cost of memory and increase the capacity while compared to Redis' with no measurement. kvrocks-website blog posts 2021-2024 (bitmap on RocksDB, how we use RocksDB, 2023 review, TLP graduation, KQIR) have no baseline comparison; the only figure is a RocksDB hash-index tuning note (21.8% less CPU, 10% more throughput, 4.6% more space) against Kvrocks without that option. The old README performance section, per a search snippet, shows Kvrocks-only redis-benchmark charts (Xeon E5-2650 v4, 48 cores) with no Redis, Pika or SSDB columns. Issue #322 'any benchmark against redis?': the maintainer says a direct comparison makes little sense and Kvrocks would 'likely' beat Redis on throughput for many commands, with no numbers; the only numbers are a user's redis-benchmark runs on DigitalOcean in which Kvrocks is not faster than KeyDB (4 vCPU shared, 8 GB NVMe, 10 threads: SET 34,352 vs 59,066 req/s, GET 56,786 vs 56,689 req/s) and no Redis run. Issue #99 reports Kvrocks writes slower than ledis, ssdb or redix, no numbers. Web searches found no third-party Redis, Pika or SSDB comparison. The guessed SQLite baseline is wrong (real peers are Redis, KeyDB, Pika, SSDB). Directional memory-cost claim only.

name: libpqxx
listed_description: The official C++ client API for PostgreSQL.
reason: Directional claims only, no numbers. NEWS for 7.8.0 and the GitHub 7.8.0 release say 'Streaming large data sets now benchmarks faster than similar C/libpq code!' with no figures; include/pqxx/doc/streams.md gives only qualitative toy-benchmark notes (a hundred or a thousand one-integer rows: streaming slower than exec; ten thousand rows: streaming faster; four-column rows: 'considerably faster' at a thousand rows) with no timings; tools/benchmark.cxx (added in 8.0.2) compares raw libpq, exec() and stream() but the repo publishes no results; issue searches found no timing comparison against libpq (#770 is about iterator copy cost only). The guessed SQLite baseline is wrong: the only relevant baseline is raw libpq, and a wrapper is not otherwise claimed to be faster. Repo is BSD-3-Clause, 1.4k stars.

name: LMDB++
listed_description: C++11 wrapper for the LMDB embedded database library.
reason: Header-only C++11 wrapper (lmdb++.h) over LMDB, public domain (Unlicense), 288 stars. The README makes only a design claim: the procedural interface 'is implemented entirely using static inline functions, so there are no hidden extra costs'. No benchmark, no measured overhead against raw LMDB, and no benchmark directory (root: etc, check.cc, example.cc, lmdb++.h, Makefile). A zero-overhead wrapper is not a faster implementation of anything; the only faster-than claims about LMDB itself belong to LMDB, which is listed separately.

name: mgclient
reason: Bolt client library for Memgraph (Apache-2.0, 44 stars). README and repo (.github, cmake, examples, include, mgclient_cpp, src, tests, tool, wasm) contain no benchmark or performance claim. Memgraph's published comparisons against Neo4j (Benchgraph/mgBench, 'Memgraph vs Neo4j: A Performance Comparison', snippet only, memgraph.com not opened) measure the database server through a C++ Bolt client, not mgclient against another driver. A web search found no mgclient versus Neo4j Bolt driver comparison. The guessed Neo4j baseline does not apply to a client library. The Memgraph server (memgraph/memgraph) is the project that carries the Neo4j claims.
